say.text: This part is about who needs an operation, when, and how to keep the bile duct safe. Do you already know the qualifiers?

choices.label: Yes, take me to the fast check
No, let me work the cases

say.text: Which statement about acalculous cholecystitis is correct?

choices.label: It runs milder, since no stone blocks the duct
Stasis and ischaemia in a critically ill patient cause it
It is managed like calculous disease, by immediate cholecystectomy
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Acalculous cholecystitis comes from stasis and ischaemia after major surgery, trauma, burns, sepsis or long fasting. It is more often gangrenous and perforated than calculous disease.
That choice is not right.
Without a stone the wall still suffers stasis and ischaemia, and gangrene and perforation are commoner than in calculous disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure. No stone does not mean a gentler disease, so the confident idea needs a second look.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The patients who get it are critically ill, so they are usually drained first and not rushed to an operation.

sure_note.text: You were sure. In the critically ill, setting and fitness decide the first step, not the diagnosis name.

say.text: Ask what injures the gallbladder wall when there is no stone, and how sick these patients are.
Think of the wall, not the duct. In a very sick patient the gallbladder empties poorly and its blood supply falls, so it can die without any stone. That is why it is the more dangerous form.
A 46-year-old man has a health check for fatty liver. Ultrasound shows gallstones. He has never had pain, fever or jaundice.
Make your call before I explain it. What do you do for these stones?

choices.label: Expectant management, with clinic review later
Ursodeoxycholic acid tablets to dissolve them
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. About 80% of gallstones never cause symptoms, and the yearly risk of trouble is only about 1 to 2%. He needs no treatment, and he comes back if symptoms begin.
That choice is not right.
Most silent stones stay silent, so an operation adds surgical risk for little gain.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the habit. A confident operation for a silent stone is the error to unlearn.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The drug dissolves only small cholesterol stones in a working gallbladder, and a silent stone needs no treatment at all.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Dissolution is a narrow indication, so check stone type, size and gallbladder function before any tablet.

say.text: Ask whether these stones are doing anything to this man right now.
Picture a hundred people with silent stones. Only one or two a year start to have trouble, so the other ninety-odd would have had an operation for nothing. You act on symptoms, not on the stone.
Which asymptomatic patient is a genuine case for prophylactic cholecystectomy, removing a stone before it causes trouble?

choices.label: A patient with a porcelain gallbladder on scan
A 30-year-old woman with a single 2 cm stone
An obese man with several small stones on scan
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. A porcelain gallbladder carries a raised risk of cancer, and it is one of the selected high-risk features. Ordinary silent stones are not an indication on their own.
That choice is not right.
A silent 2 cm stone carries a low yearly risk, and size counts only above 3 cm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again at size. A 2 cm silent stone does not reach the threshold.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Several small silent stones carry the same low yearly risk as one, so the count is not the test.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The number of stones is not the test, so look for a named high-risk feature.

say.text: Think about the one feature that makes a silent gallbladder dangerous, not the size or number of the stones.
The test is a named high-risk feature, not the stone. Porcelain wall, stones over 3 cm, a polyp over 1 cm and sickle cell disease qualify. A 2 cm stone or a handful of small ones meet none of these.
Which patient's stones are most likely to dissolve on ursodeoxycholic acid?

choices.label: A large calcified stone in a healthy gallbladder
Black pigment stones seen in chronic haemolysis
Small cholesterol stones in a working gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Dissolution works only on small, radiolucent cholesterol stones, and only when the gallbladder still fills and empties. Stones often return once the drug is stopped.
That choice is not right.
Dissolution works on small radiolucent cholesterol stones, so a large calcified stone is outside the rule.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Calcified stones are outside what the drug can dissolve, so the confident pick needs revising.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Pigment stones are not the cholesterol type, so the drug does not touch them.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Pigment stones are the type dissolution does not touch, a common misconception.

say.text: Ask what the drug is made to dissolve: which stone type, which size, and what the gallbladder must still do.
Three questions before any tablet. What is the stone made of, how big is it, and does the gallbladder still empty? Only a small cholesterol stone in a working gallbladder passes all three.

A 58-year-old man is ventilated in the intensive care unit after a long laparotomy for trauma. He has fever and right upper quadrant tenderness. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with no stone.
He is too unwell for a long operation. What is the first step?

choices.label: Immediate open cholecystectomy to remove the source
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. A critically ill patient with no stone is the setting for acalculous disease, which comes from stasis and ischaemia. Drainage is the safe first step while he is too sick for an operation.
That choice is not right.
In critically ill patients without stones the disease comes from stasis and ischaemia, and he cannot safely tolerate a long operation now.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The sure operation is the trap here, because the setting and his fitness decide the first step.

say.text: That choice is not right.
An unfit ventilated patient cannot safely have a major operation now, open or laparoscopic, so first make him safe.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Operating first is the habit to unlearn in a patient too unwell for surgery.

say.text: Start with how sick he is and whether a stone is present, then ask what he can tolerate right now.
Two facts decide it. He has no stone, so the cause is stasis and ischaemia. He is ventilated, so he is too ill for theatre. Drainage treats the gallbladder without that operative stress.
A 66-year-old woman is three weeks into parenteral nutrition after a bowel resection. She has fever and right upper pain. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled gallbladder and no stone.
Her team plans to leave it for several days. What is the main risk to plan around?

choices.label: Early cholecystectomy today, to remove the source of risk
A mild course, because no stone blocks the duct
Gangrene and perforation, from stasis and ischaemia
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Long parenteral nutrition is a classic setting for stasis and ischaemia. Acalculous disease is more often gangrenous and perforated than calculous disease, and its mortality is higher.
That choice is not right.
A woman this unwell is not ready for an operation today, so the safe plan is drainage first, with surgery later.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check fitness before you choose the operation.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Acalculous disease has no stone to blame, yet it is the more dangerous form, not the milder one.

sure_note.text: You were sure. No stone means no obstruction, but stasis still injures the wall.

say.text: Think about what happens to a gallbladder wall when its blood supply is poor and it is not drained.
Follow the wall. Without feeding the gallbladder stops emptying, and a sick patient's blood supply to it falls. A stagnant, underperfused wall can die, so waiting is the risk.
Two structures are now seen entering the gallbladder. What else must be true before you clip, for a safe critical view?

choices.label: Cystic duct dissected alone down to the bile duct
Nothing more; the two-structure count completes the view
Triangle cleared; lower gallbladder off the liver bed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. The critical view needs three things: the triangle cleared of fat and fibrous tissue, the lower gallbladder separated from the cystic plate, and two structures seen entering. Two structures alone are not enough.
That choice is not right.
Working down the duct before the triangle is clear removes the margin that makes the view safe.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Working down the duct early removes the margin the view depends on.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Two structures can be seen while the triangle is still full of fat, so the count alone does not prove a safe view.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The count is the last check, not the whole test.

say.text: The memorable count is the last of three requirements. Ask what must be cleared before anything can be counted.
Think of a checklist with three ticks. Clear triangle, lower gallbladder off the plate, then the two-structure count. The count is the last tick, and it means little if the first two are blank.
Which order is safe for the steps before clipping in laparoscopic cholecystectomy?

choices.label: Confirm two structures first, then clear the triangle, clip
Divide the first tubular structure seen, then confirm
Clear the triangle, separate the gallbladder, confirm, clip
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Clear the triangle first, separate the lower gallbladder from the plate, confirm the two structures, and only then clip. The order is what makes the count meaningful.
That choice is not right.
The count means little until the triangle is cleared, so the check comes last.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The count comes last, because it means little until the area is clear.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The first tube seen may be the bile duct, so you confirm before dividing anything.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Dividing the first tube seen is the habit that causes duct injury.

say.text: Ask which step makes the next one trustworthy: a structure can only be counted once the area around it is clear.
Each step makes the next one trustworthy. You cannot count structures in a crowded triangle, and you cannot trust a clip until the count is honest. So the order runs clear, separate, confirm, clip.
At laparoscopy, dense inflammation fuses the hepatocystic triangle and you cannot clear it.
What is the safe move?

choices.label: Clip the two structures you can see, then carry on
Divide the first tube you find, to gain control
Bail out by subtotal cholecystectomy or conversion
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. When the triangle cannot be dissected safely, subtotal cholecystectomy or conversion to open surgery is the safe bail-out. You do not clip structures you cannot identify.
That choice is not right.
Two visible structures do not prove the view when the triangle cannot be cleared, so clipping on a count is unsafe.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A count does not replace a cleared triangle, even when time is passing.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The first tube found may be the bile duct, and dividing it is the commonest route to major duct injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Taking the first tube for the cystic duct is the mistake behind most duct injuries.

say.text: Ask what you may not do when the view cannot be reached, and which operations avoid the triangle.

Safety here is not finishing the planned operation but avoiding the duct. If the triangle will not clear, the view cannot be reached, so you change the operation: remove the gallbladder in part, or convert.
What is the commonest cause of a major bile duct injury during cholecystectomy?

choices.label: Bleeding from the cystic artery during dissection
Injury to the right hepatic artery in the triangle
Misidentifying the bile duct as the cystic duct
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Most major duct injuries come from misidentification, when the bile duct is taken for the cystic duct and divided. That is why the critical view comes before clipping.
That choice is not right.
Bleeding is a different problem, and the commonest duct injury comes from mistaken anatomy, not from a vessel.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Bleeding is the dramatic complication, but the commonest duct injury is a mistaken identity.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The cystic artery is usually its branch, but the commonest duct injury is misidentification, not an arterial injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The right hepatic artery is close to the duct, but misidentification is the commonest cause.

say.text: Think about the most common error in identifying anatomy, not the most dramatic complication.

Think of the tube that looks right but is wrong. The common bile duct can be pulled into the field and mistaken for the cystic duct. Divide it, and you have a major injury. The view exists to prevent that.
The rule: most stones are silent and need no treatment. Grade, fitness and the setting decide the operation, and an unfit or acalculous patient is drained first.
The duct is protected by the view, not by a count of structures.
